name: Middle English Period
description: The literature of England from the aftermath of the Norman Conquest to the eve of the sixteenth century, composed in Middle English (with major parallel corpora in Latin and Anglo-Norman French). The period spans the slow re-emergence of the English vernacular as a literary language in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, the great flowering of the age of Chaucer and his contemporaries (c. 1350–1400), and the fifteenth-century consolidation of a national literary culture in the hands of Chaucerians, Scottish makars, devotional writers, dramatists, and the first English printers.
historical_context: The Norman Conquest (1066) imposed a French-speaking ruling class and made Latin and Anglo-Norman the languages of record, demoting English for a century and a half; yet the English of the East Midlands and London gradually re-emerged as the common literary medium, decisively reinforced by the loss of Normandy (1204), the Provisions of Oxford (1258), the Hundred Years War (1337–1453), the Black Death (1348–49) and its social aftershocks (the Statute of Labourers 1351, the Peasants' Revolt 1381), the deposition of Richard II (1399), and the Lancastrian and Yorkist struggles culminating in the Wars of the Roses (1455–1485) and the Tudor accession (1485). The church provided the institutional framework for most literary production until the Wycliffite movement (c. 1380–1430) challenged its authority in the vernacular; the foundation of schools and the Inns of Court, the rise of London as capital, the establishment of English as the language of parliament and law, and the introduction of printing by William Caxton (1476) all consolidated English as a national literary language.
literary_characteristics: Middle English literature is exceptionally various: alliterative verse survives and is revived in the West and North (the Alliterative Revival), while the French-derived rhymed couplet and stanza become the dominant poetic forms; prose develops from the devotional treatises of the AB language group through Wycliffite biblical translation to the mature prose of Malory and Caxton; romance, lyric, dream vision, debate, satire, drama (mystery, miracle, and morality plays), chronicle, hagiography, and mystical and devotional writing all flourish. Major manuscripts — Cotton Nero A.x (the Pearl manuscript), Auchinleck, Harley 2253, the Vernon manuscript, the Thornton manuscript — preserve much of the poetic record, and the works of Geoffrey Chaucer, William Langland, the Gawain-poet, John Gower, Thomas Malory, and the Scottish makars constitute the period's canonical centre.
